svg.font-family: 'Source Code Pro', ui-monospace, SFMono-Regular, Menlo, monospace
svg.aria-label: The MSEQ clock control loop: measure the gap between incoming ticks, compute the ideal position from tick counts, rate and offset, then correct the next output wait by ten per cent of the error, capped at one millisecond per tick.
svg.text: The fix: MSEQ runs its own clock and steers it
A flywheel. MSEQ emits its own even tick stream, compares it with Ableton's, and
trims the next wait by a fraction of the difference — never by more than a hair.
1 · measure what arrived
Δ = gap since the previous F8, from [timer]
in_ticks = in_ticks + 1
in_phase = in_phase + Δ
Every tick, however odd its gap. This is evidence, not a trigger.
2 · work out where MSEQ ought to be by now
rate = 2500 / BPM — Ableton's tempo, as CC 99 + CC 98
or the mean gap over the last 48 ticks, if no tempo is sent
ideal = in_phase + (out_ticks − in_ticks) × rate + offset
error = out_phase − ideal — positive means MSEQ is late
Counting both streams is what lets a wanted offset be held rather
than mistaken for an error, and a gap in delivery pass harmlessly.
3 · adjust the next wait, a little
delay = rate − 0.1 × error, capped at ±1 ms per tick
pd.Clock waits that long, then bangs counter 0 143.
MSEQ's own clock decides when every step fires; Ableton only ever
nudges its speed. Delivery noise cannot reach the notes directly.
out_ticks, out_phase
one tick at 140 BPM, to scale
±1 ms — all the loop may move it
Measured over 17 minutes against a 140 BPM master: phase error median +2.6 ms
(sd 0.9 ms) and total drift +2 to +3 ms, not growing, from 2.5 ms of input jitter.
